sections.lesson:
### Segment 6 — The Lesson
Simple, low-friction signals tend to become the dominant currency in any system that measures them, because they are cheap to produce and easy to compare. When those signals are attached to human identity rather than to the content itself, they reshape behavior at scale. Designers and policymakers therefore face a recurring choice: either accept that the metric will drive the activity, or deliberately limit how visible and consequential the metric is allowed to become.

sections.lesson:
### Segment 6 — The Lesson
Incentive structures that rely on observable proxies will eventually be gamed once the stakes become high enough. Complex ranking systems therefore require continuous redesign, and each redesign shifts the target rather than eliminating the underlying dynamic. When designing any measurement that will influence behavior, it is worth asking what new activity will become rational once the measure itself is widely known and acted upon.
